author: Rahul kp
title: Permutation
simple_words: Permutation is arranging, where order counts. Combination is selecting, where order does not count.

definitions.meaning: Number of ways of arranging r items out of n different items, where the ==order matters==.
Number of ways of selecting r items out of n different items, where the ==order does not matter==.
definitions.note: ABC and BAC are the same

key_points: Words like arrange, line up, rank, form a number, seat point to ==permutation==.
Words like select, choose, committee, team, hand of cards point to ==combination==.
!!Ask first: if I swap two items, is it a new result?!! Yes means permutation, no means combination.
For the same n and r, nPr is never less than nCr.
formula_hook: same n, same r, one extra r!

formulas.name: Permutation
formulas.legend: n = total different items, r = items taken at a time, n! = n × (n−1) × … × 1, 0! = 1

formulas.name: Combination
formulas.legend: n = total different items, r = items chosen. Also nCr = nC(n−r)

formulas.name: Link between the two
formulas.legend: First select r items (nCr), then arrange them in r! ways

insight.text: Permutation is a combination whose chosen items are then arranged, so it is larger by the factor r!.

trick_hook: P for Position, C for Committee

memory_trick.explanation: Positions like President and Secretary differ, so order counts (P). In a committee all members are equal, so order does not count (C).

steps: Check r ≤ n and answer is whole
exam_tip: Cancel factorials before multiplying. Write n! as n × (n−1)! so the big terms cut out and the sums stay small.

doubt.question: Why is nPr bigger than nCr?
doubt.answer: Each chosen group of r items can be arranged in r! ways, so nPr = nCr × r!. They are equal only when r = 0 or r = 1.

mistakes.wrong: Using nCr to form a 3-digit number or to arrange people in a row
mistakes.right: When order gives a different result (numbers, ranks, seating), use nPr.

mistakes.wrong: Using nPr to select a committee or a team
mistakes.right: Selection with no order and no distinct roles needs nCr.

mistakes.wrong: Calculating nCr for r larger than n
mistakes.right: r cannot exceed n, as you cannot select more items than are available.

check_notes: Checker 1: Exam tip: 'so the big terms cut out and the sums stay small' – 'sums' is loose, because the work is multiplication and division. Better: 'so the large factorial terms cancel and the calculation stays small.'
Checker 1: Key point 1: 'form a number' leads to nPr only when the digits are not repeated. Better: 'form a number (digits not repeated)'. If repetition is allowed, the count is n^r, not nPr.
